elements.element: Customer has no non-compete or field-of-use restriction.
elements.evidence: Revised Section 12.4 now reads "Customer is not restricted from developing, marketing, selling, or acquiring any product or service that competes with Vendor in any territory." The prohibitory "shall not develop, market, sell, or acquire" language and the 24-month post-term tail are gone; Section 12.3 is retained and independently confirms Customer "has made no exclusivity, non-compete, most-favoured-customer, minimum-volume, or no-hire commitment." No field-of-use, territory, or product restriction binds Customer anywhere in the rendered language.

elements.element: The restriction covers only a named competing product.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: no restriction on Customer survives the edit, so there is nothing to narrow to a named product. The fallback's purpose (contain an existing restriction) is exceeded by full removal at the preferred level.

elements.element: The restriction applies during the term only.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the term-plus-twenty-four-months tail was deleted and no restriction of any duration remains, so there is no period to confine to the term.

elements.element: The restriction lasts no longer than 12 months.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the 24-month post-term duration was removed entirely; no durational covenant remains to measure against the 12-month cap.

elements.element: The restriction permits Customer's internal development.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: revised 12.4 affirmatively confirms Customer may develop competing products or services, and 12.3 preserves Customer's freedom to develop any product or service, so no carve-out is required.
Condition does not apply: the bar on acquiring competing products/services was struck; revised 12.4 and retained 12.3 both confirm Customer may acquire any product or service.

reasons: Preferred level is complete: the sole preferred element is met because the operative restriction in Section 12.4 has been converted from a prohibition into a confirmation that Customer is unrestricted, and no other field-of-use, territory, product, or competing-business restraint binds Customer in the rendered text.

The fallback checklist is vacuously satisfied because each fallback element presupposes a surviving restriction; removal at the preferred level disposes of the condition for all five, and none of them is left dependent on an undefined trigger.

Minimality holds: the edit touches only Section 12.4, the clause targeted by the rule, leaves Section 12.3's Customer-favourable freedom-of-action and no-commitment acknowledgement untouched, and adds no survival tail, procedure, damages category, or other extra requirement outside the checklist. The residual overlap between revised 12.4 and 12.3 is a neutral, non-contradictory confirmation rather than a competing operative obligation, so it does not amount to duplicated operative terms; a bare deletion of 12.4 would also have been acceptable.

Intent is preserved: no defined term is orphaned, no cross-reference dangles (nothing else in the cited text refers to 12.4's covenant), and the retained Section 12.3 is now consistent rather than contradicted, curing the internal conflict that existed in the original.

Comment is compliant in tone and content: it states the change and the reason in two sentences, cites the playbook position, and offers the narrowed fallback (single named product, term only, internal-development and acquisition carve-outs) without lecturing.
